summary: BLM lookout in Baker County: a 1957 temporary station, then a 1963 cab on a 10-ft concrete base; firelookout.com says the cab is available for emergencies.

facts.design: BLM design cabin similar to the USFS R6 Flat Top, on a 10-ft concrete base, with a wooden live-in cab (1963)

access.note: Bureau of Land Management land. Firelookout.com says the cab is available for emergencies. No public visiting rules were found.

events.note: Temporary lookout placed on the mountain; the NHLR says temporary lookouts stayed until the permanent structure was built.
A June 1958 newspaper item says the BLM would man the new station starting July 1.
BLM was considering an access road into the area and a proposed station that would include a power line.
Present BLM design cab on a 10-ft concrete base with a wooden live-in cab.
Two members of the summer BLM fire crew took shifts manning the tower, per a 1975 newspaper item.
Registered June 22, 2022; nominated by Brad Eells.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Firelookout.com dates a cabin on the site to the 1930s. The NHLR and Forest Lookouts start with a 1957 temporary lookout. Every source dates the present cab to 1963, which the record keeps.
The record's 3.0 m matches the 10-ft concrete base only. No source gives a total tower height, so facts.height_m is left out. Consider whether the record's height field should be cleared.

sources.title: Big Lookout Mtn. Fire Lookout Tower

notes_for_editor: Access 'restricted' is inferred from firelookout.com's 'available for emergencies' (undated); no 2020s source confirms current use. The 2010 peakbagging photo caption (dated July 16, 2010) says the lookout was staffed by two people; the names are left out of the story. Elevation was not reconciled: NHLR gives 2,172 m (matches the record), firelookout.com gives 7120 ft, peakbagging gives 7126 ft. The record's height_m of 3.0 m is only the 10-ft base; check it before publishing a height. The 1975 and 1962 items come from newspaper excerpts on the Forest Lookouts page, not the newspapers themselves.
